full_judgment:
Mr. Shah Abu Naveen Mominur Rahman: The instant appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated 29.5.2005 passed in Misc. Case No.27 of 2002, arising out of an application for granting of probate under Act No. XXXIX of 1925, passed by the learned District Judge, Feni. 

 3. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the appeal arc that one Brojendra Lal Poddar, made an will dated 31.12.76 in favour of his sons Sukhomoy Poddar. Rasomay Poddar and Pritimoy Poddar in respect of immoveable properties, owned and possessed by him, and said Brojendra Lal Poddar died on 21.12.88 and that he, during his life time and subsequent to creation of die will, transferred 20 decimals of land, which he did not disclose, and that the application for granting probate was filed in Court on 3.11.03 and objection was raised there-against in the written objection it has been disclosed that out of the 'ka' schedule land of the apart from transfer of 20 decimals of land vide 9 sale-deeds dated 03.11.88, further 2 decimals of land' was gifted in favour of the opposite party-respondent No.1 on 20.3.86. Therefore the so far it relates to schedule-Ka land, became in executable, as all lands there under have been exhausted, and therefore no probate can be granted as prayed for. Further there is a litigation pending in the Court of Assistant Judge, Feni, Sadar, being Partition Suit No.91 of 2000 in respect of the land covered by the will, and the parties thereof are contesting the case by filing written statement. 

 5. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submitted that the Court below has erred in law on misreading and misconstruing the provisions of law, in that the application for probate relaters to the "issue" whether there is any existence of a 'will' or not and granting of probate certificate is not directly related only to the properties covered by the 'will' and that if there remains any portion of the properties, detailed in the 'will'. the Court is under obligation to grant probate as prayed for, provided the 'will' is proved to be genuine and that the beneficiary will take recourse to get benefit out of the 'will', and that in the instant case there are 3 schedules, of land given in the 'will' and that the .appellant claimed interest only in the 'ka' schedule of the and the said 'ka' schedule land consists of 24 decimals of land and therefore, if for the sake of argument it is admitted that the Executor has transferred 22 decimals of land, yet there remains balance of 2 decimals of land and therefore the petitioner has cause of action for probate for dealing with the said 2 decimals of land and accordingly he is entitled to pray for granting probate. The learned Advocate submitted that in view of the decisions given by the Superior Courts of the subcontinent, there is no limitation prescribed for the purpose of making application for granting probate under the Succession Act. 1925 and that Article 181 of the limitation Act. 1908 is not attracted in case of application filed for granting of probate. The learned Advocate referring to some decisions of the Indian jurisdiction submitted that after the amendment of the Indian limitation Act in 1963 the applications for "granting probate and letter of administration", have been covered by Article- 137 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, which law is different from the Article 181 of our Limitation .Act, 1908, inasmuch as the Limitation Act of 1908 basically relates to the suits and applications covered by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The learned Advocate relied in the decisions in the case of Kerala S.E. Board Vs. T.P. Kunhaliumma reported in AIR,1977 (SC)282 and in the case of Shobha Vs. Janki reported in AIR 1987 145, wherein the some cases of Indian Supreme Court including the case reported in AIR 1977 SC 282, have been discussed and it has been held that the . Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to any petition or application filed under any Act filed in any Civil Court and the same is not confined to applications contemplated by or under the Code of Civil Procedure and that the Limitation Act. 1908 deals with such suits and applications as are contemplated under the Code of Civil Procedure and thus an application for granting probate do not come under the purview of Limitation Act. 1908 and for that matter is not regulated by the provisions of Article 181 thereof. 

 6. The learned Advocate then submitted that, as has been held by the Superior Courts of the Subcontinent, once the application of limitation starts it cannot be stopped, and that limitation starts from the date of accrual of the cause of action and in the case of grant of probate the cause of action subsists on each day, so long the property covered by the 'will' exists. The- learned Advocate in elaborating his submissions stated that the probate certificate authorises the beneficiary to deal with the properties mentioned in the 'will' and therefore the cause of action continues till properties are not exhausted, provided no probate has been granted earlier. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondent found it difficult to resist the appeal having had found that after transfer of 22 decimals of land there remained 2 decimals of land in which the petitioner-appellant claim his interest on the basis of the 'will'. We appreciate the gesture of the learned Advocate for placing the case of Ramanand Thakur Vs. Parmananda Thakur, reported in AIR 1982 Patna 87, which we found to be beneficial since in the said judgment a large number of decisions relating to granting of probate under the Succession  Act, in particular relating to limitation for filing an application therefore, have been considered. In the said decision their lordships have made the following observation:- 

 "Article 137 of the new Limitation Act is the residuary Article like Art. 181 of the old Limitation Act but with certain modification in the language and its classification which in our view is of great importance Article 181 was placed in the Third Division dealing with the application, but Art. 137 has been placed separately although under the Third Division in a separate part to govern "other applications" apparently thereby indicating the intention of the legislature that the expression application was not confined to the types of cases where the other articles under the. Third Division were placed. Apart from the change of the division, the words used in A. 137 are also slightly different. The words any other ‘application’ under Art. 137 cannot be said on the principle of ejusdem generis applies only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure other than those mentioned in Part-I of the Third Division. In the old Limitation Act the word "application" was not defined and all that was defined was the express "applicant". The changed definition of the words "applicant" and introduction of the definition of the word "application" in S. 2 (a) and 2 (b) of the 1963 Act indicates the object of the Limitation Act to include petitions under special laws other than the Code of Civil Procedure. It was on this account that the operation of Art. 181 was limited to 'applications made under the Civil Procedure Code particularly in view of the fact that all the other applications in the division in which Article 181 was placed referred to the applications under the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, almost all the High Courts including the Supreme Court had taken the view that the "application" referred to in Article 181, by the application of the doctrine of ejusdem generis applied only to the applications under the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 The Supreme Court in the case of Kerala S.E. Board v. T.P. Kunhaliumma, (AIR 1977 SC 282) has noticed the differences pointed out above and has overruled its earlier view that Art. 137 applied only to application made under the Code of Civil Procedure. But notwithstanding the taking of this view of the legal position regarding the construction of Art.137, the petitioner in our considered opinion still must fail inasmuch as in the case of the application for grant of Probate or Letters of Administration, it is difficult to find out as to when the right to apply accrues because unless that date can be fixed, there is no question of starting of the period of limitation. Although we could not find any decision on this question of our own High Court, we find this question having been discussed by a Bench of the Calcutta High Court in tile case of Kalinath v. Nagendra oath. (AIR 1959 Ca1.8 1) though it was a case under the old Limitation Act where the learned Judges were confronted with Art.181 of the Limitation Act. The argument advanced in the case was that the starting point for computing the period of limitation would be the date when the executor for the first time became aware of the will. This argument was rejected as Mr. Madhusudan Singh had contended that the starting date for the said purpose would be the date of the death of the testator. We are unable to accept this contention as the right to apply for a probate accrues from day to clay so long as the will remains unprofaned. In other words the right to apply accrues every day and the cause of action for an application for probate arises every moment so long as the will remains unprofaned and, therefore, for such an application' there is no period of limitation and for taking this view we find full support from the Calcutta case which also finds support from the view taken by the Madras High Court in the case of Gnanamuthu Upadesi. v. Yana Koilpillai Nadan, (1894) ILR 17 Mad. 379). Therefore, while holding .that the Art. 137 of the new Limitation Act applies to any petition or application filed under any Act, we do not feel any, difficulty to come to the conclusion that so far as the application for grant of a Probate or Letters of Administration is concerned they are not governed by any Article of the Limitation Act," 

 8. We are in respectful agreement with the discussions and observations, made in the decision, as quoted above. Accordingly we find substance on the submissions made by the learned Advocate appearing that the petitioner-appellant that the cause of action to apply for granting probate in the instant case accrues every day, since the cause of action for an application for probate subsists every moment, so long as the 'will' remains unprofaned and the properties exist and that for such application there is no period of limitation. Thus having regard to the fact that there remained 2 decimals of land in the 'ka' schedule land of the 'will' to which the petitioner claims interest and there being no specific limitation for making application for granting Probate, subject to existence of properties covered the we find merit in the appeal. 

 9. Accordingly the appeal is allowed without any order to cost. The impugned order dated 29.5.05 passed in Misc. Case No.27/2002 by the District Judge. Feni, rejecting the prayer of granting of probate is set aside. The prayer of probate is allowed. The learned District Judge, Feni, is directed to issue certificate granting probate, as prayed for, in accordance with law.
